summaries.summary: RNN-based neural translation models use about 5% of traditional shallow SMT memory, jointly train modules, but require heavy corpora, harming morphologically rich language translation.
MT efficiency depends on parallel corpus availability and size and syntactic divergence, with English-like fusional languages differing from agglutinative morphologically rich languages.
Agglutination creates many Tamil inflectional forms, including at least 30,000 verb forms and about 5,000 noun forms, hiding meanings and increasing MT complexity.
Tamil translation is difficult because parallel corpus availability is very scarce and most English–Tamil MT corpora were manually created and unavailable online.
Tamil pronunciation-based suffix characters, unique for each consonant, degrade MT because words with different suffixes are treated as different words in training.
Tamil has written and spoken forms, increasing corpus vocabulary with two versions, as seen between Bible traditional Tamil and movie subtitle spoken Tamil.
Building an English–Tamil neural MT system requires a trade-off between domain specificity and size of the corpus.
The experiment corpus combined EnTam v2, TDIL tourism data, and AU-KBC Tamil novels and short stories, totaling 197,792 sentences.
A self-collected monolingual Tamil corpus of 567,772 sentences supported word2vec embeddings and a phrase-based SMT language model, standardized to UTF-8 and cleaned.
Source and target word embeddings initialize model vectors, and the word2vec skip gram model optimizes vectors using average log probability of context words.
The formulation defines k, corpus words, training corpus size, hierarchical softmax probability, and omits negative sampling and subsampling of frequent words.
A monolingual corpus of 569,772 Tamil sentences was used to create semantically meaningful word embeddings with greater contextual richness.
The word2vec model used vector size 100, window size 5, 7 worker threads, batch size 50 words, negative sampling 1, and gensim.
The Bahdanau2014 model uses a bidirectional LSTM encoder, context vector, and attention-based decoder with weighted encoder outputs and previous decoded words.
Neural Machine Translation computes target sentence probability word by word, with basic and attention-based decoders differing in their log probability calculations.
The attention formulation defines target sentence length, target and source sentences, fixed encoder output vector, and weighted encoder hidden outputs as attention vector.
The decoder LSTM computes: DISPLAYFORM0.
Decoder probability depends on previous output, current hidden layer vector, and attention context vector, which is a weighted sum over the sentence.
The context vector uses source tokens, encoder hidden values, and alignment parameters from a feed forward neural network trained jointly with the translation model.
Softmax feedforward outputs, decoder hidden states, encoder annotations, and concatenated forward and reverse encoder hidden parameters compute attention weights for overall sentence context.
Global attention is preferred over local attention because English–Tamil structural discordance and morphological and structural variations make local lookup inefficient.
The No Peepholes (NP) LSTM variant from Greff et al. greff2015lstm uses gated cell and hidden vectors to prevent vanishing gradients.
The decoder uses equations 7 through 11, while the encoder uses a bidirectional RNN LSTM with forward and backward hidden layer components.
Morphological segmentation uses a semi-supervised extension of a generative probabilistic model maximizing MAP probability of recursive prefix,root,postfix word splits.
Each training lexicon word is included, the prior uses the Minimum Description Length(MDL) principle, and the likelihood is estimated separately.
Intermediate analyses and the INLINEFORM2 morpheme of word INLINEFORM3 are defined for the likelihood estimation.
An extended Viterbi algorithm decodes using exhaustive morpheme mapping, with extra parameters and a cost function addressing over-segmentation and under-segmentation.
The cost function includes likelihoods for the cost function, annotated dataset contribution, and labeled data, with parameters controlling segment size and corpus discrepancies.
The Python extension to morfessor 2.0 performed segmentation using Tamil annotation data from Anoop Kunchukkutan in the Indic NLP Library.
English to Tamil translation used an RNN LSTM Bi-directional encoder attention decoder architecture, with phrase based SMT, Factored SMT reference, and 569,772 monolingual Tamil sentences.
Training sentences were bucketed by fixed sizes to minimize PAD tokens, with more buckets around 10–20 words and RNNMorph target buckets increased uniformly by 5.
RNNSearch vocabularies were restricted to 60,000 out of 67,768 English and 150,000 out of 340,325 Tamil words, while RNNMorph used 67,768 English and 41,906 Tamil words.
The model used SGD, sampled softmax loss of 512 per sample, learning rate 1.0, decay rate 0.5, gradient clipping global norm 5.0, and Tensorflow seq2seq.
Evaluation used BLEU modified 1-gram, 2-gram, 3-gram and 4-gram precision values and human metrics of adequacy, fluency and relative ranking values.
The BLEU scores obtained using the various models used in the experiment are tabulated in Table TABREF25.
BLEU computes micro-averaged unigram, bigram, trigram and BLEU-4 precision values, with phrase-based SMT inferior to RNNSearch and word2vec slightly increasing BLEU scores.
Morphological segmentation improved RNNMorph BLEU precision values, but increased tokens from Tamil segmentation may inflate the numeric BLEU increase.
Human evaluation used adequacy, precision and ranking values, 50 native annotators, about 100 randomized test sentences, 5-point scales, and intra-annotator values.
The human evaluation Kappa co-efficient results are calculated with respect to DISPLAYFORM0.
Ranking Kappa co-efficient was 0.573 for RNNMorph and 0.410 for RNNSearch+Word2Vec, implying annotators found RNNMorph produced better results.
RNNMorph learning rate decay was manual after specific epochs, with earlier perplexity saturation and target vocabulary reduced from 340,325 words to 41,906 morphs.
Sampled SoftMax loss accommodated a large target vocabulary, and Fig. FIGREF35 shows RNNMorph consistently better perplexity values with 4 hidden layers.

Attention vectors show reduced vocabulary improved source sentence lookup, while RNNSearch with Word2Vec embeddings attended to INLINEFORM4 EOS INLINEFORM5 and used only 44% Tamil and 74% English vocabulary.
Morphological segmentation of Tamil text decreased target vocabulary size from 340,325 to 41,906, reducing unknown tokens and dividing vocabulary into morphological roots and inflections.
RNNMorph translations sometimes repeat phrases, possibly due to increased target sequence length, more morphs per sentence, and semi-supervised morphological segmentation errors.
RNNSearch + Word2Vec and Morph2Vec outputs show morphological segmentation improves grammatical soundness, with most Morph2Vec translations having no INLINEFORM0 UNK INLINEFORM1 tokens.
Related English–Tamil MT work includes MAT, EBMT with 700000 sentences, rule based systems, HMM-based SMT, hybrid approaches, SMT, and morphological pre and post processing techniques.
RNN Encoder Decoder models improved translation for similar grammatical structures, with Cho et al SecondOneByCho in 2014 and Sutskever et al. sutskever2014sequence using static context vectors.
Bahdanau et al. Bahdanau2014 introduced attention via variable length word vectors, and Luong et al. luong2015effective distinguished global and local attention using AER scores.
Morphological segmentation improves translation for morphologically rich languages, and both languages should be individually segmented when their agglutination schemes differ.
Morphological segmentation increases average sentence lengths and model complexity, but attention models can help, and Tamil generally has fewer words per sentence than English.
The implemented model includes only source-side morphological segmentation, so a morphological generator is essential for end-to-end translation output in words rather than morphemes.
A better corpus could generalize beyond domain specific source sentences, and a better GPU could improve hidden layer sizes, batch sizes, scope and accuracy.
Rocktaschel et al. rocktaschel2015reasoning's encoder–decoder architecture for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can be used for the same model.
The author thanks Dr. M. Anand Kumar and Dr. Arvindan for support, guidance, inputs and suggestions.
